title: Algorithms, Feeds and Digital Wellbeing
summary: What decides what you see online: how recommendation algorithms rank your feed, how they learn from your behaviour, how filter bubbles and rabbit holes form, how persuasive design competes for your attention, how to take control of your digital wellbeing, and how to design a fairer feed.
learn: What recommendation algorithms are and how they rank feeds
How recommenders use data and techniques like collaborative filtering
How filter bubbles, echo chambers and rabbit holes form
How the attention economy and persuasive design shape our behaviour
How to look after your digital wellbeing and control your feeds
How laws and better design could make feeds fairer and safer
intro: Every time you open a video app or social feed, an algorithm has chosen what you see from millions of options, in a fraction of a second, based on everything you've done before. These recommendation systems are some of the most powerful algorithms in the world. In this topic you'll find out how they work, build a recommender yourself, explore how feeds can trap us in bubbles or pull us down rabbit holes, discover the design tricks that keep us scrolling, learn how to take back control, and design a feed that's fairer to its users.

pages.title: Who chooses your feed?
pages.spec: Explain what a recommendation algorithm is, compare chronological and ranked feeds, and describe the signals algorithms use
pages.summary: A recommendation algorithm chooses and orders content for each user. Most platforms use ranked feeds instead of showing posts in time order. They predict what you'll engage with using signals such as watch time, likes, shares, comments, follows and what similar people enjoyed.
pages.starter: Open any video app in your head. Why do you think the first video it shows you is that one?
sc: I can explain what a recommendation algorithm does
I can compare chronological and ranked feeds
I can describe the signals algorithms use

b: An algorithm is a set of steps to solve a problem
A recommendation algorithm chooses what to show each person
Huge scale: billions of posts, billions of users, decisions in milliseconds
Used for videos, music, shopping, news, games and adverts
Chronological feed: newest posts first, from accounts you follow
Ranked feed: an algorithm orders posts by what it predicts you'll engage with
"For You" feeds show content from accounts you don't follow
Most big platforms default to ranked feeds
Watch time: how long you watch, and whether you rewatch
Likes, comments, shares, saves, follows
What you skip or scroll past quickly
Your device, location, time of day, language, and what similar users like

blocks.text: Recommendation algorithms

An **[[algorithm]]** is a precise set of steps to solve a problem. A **[[recommendation algorithm]]** (or recommender system) decides which content to show each person and in what order. Platforms such as TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, Spotify, Netflix and Amazon all use them. With billions of possible posts and billions of users, they must make each decision in milliseconds.
Chronological vs ranked feeds

blocks.caption: Types of feed
head: Feature
**[[chronological feed|Chronological feed]]**
**[[ranked feed|Ranked feed]]**
rows: Accounts you follow and accounts you don't ("For You")
Predictable; you won't miss recent posts from friends
Finds content you might like; can feel endless
Can be overwhelming; misses older good posts
Hard to understand; can push extreme or addictive content

blocks.text: Signals
Algorithms predict **[[engagement]]**: how likely you are to interact with a post. They learn from signals:

blocks.title: Signals recommendation algorithms use
items: Watch time and completion: did you watch to the end, or rewatch?
Interactions: likes, comments, shares, saves, follows
Negative signals: skipping, scrolling past, "not interested", reporting
Content information: hashtags, sounds, captions, what's in the image or video
Context: device, language, location, time of day
What similar users engaged with

blocks.text: Watch time is one of the most powerful signals. Even if you don't like or comment, pausing on a video tells the algorithm you're interested.

blocks.title: Feed detective
steps: Look at the two (fictional) feeds for "Cara": one chronological, one ranked.
Describe three differences.
For five posts in the ranked feed, suggest which signals made the algorithm show them.
Discuss: which feed would you prefer, and why?

q.q: Describe three differences between the two feeds.
q.a: E.g. the ranked feed includes posts from accounts Cara doesn't follow; posts are in a different order (not newest first); the ranked feed has more videos similar to ones she watched to the end.

q.q: Which signals might explain a football video appearing in Cara's ranked feed?
q.a: She watched other football videos to the end, liked a team's post, people similar to her watched it, and it's trending in her location.

o: An algorithm that chooses what content to show each person

check.q: How is a chronological feed ordered?
Which is a signal algorithms use?

o: How much people interact with content

practice.q: Explain the difference between a chronological feed and a ranked feed.
practice.a: Chronological shows newest first from accounts you follow (1); ranked uses an algorithm to order by predicted interest/engagement (1).

practice.q: Describe three signals a video app might use to decide what to recommend.
practice.a: Any three: watch time/completion (1); likes/comments/shares (1); skips/"not interested" (1); follows (1); content info (1); context (1); similar users (1).

pages.title: How recommenders learn
pages.spec: Explain how recommender systems use data, collaborative filtering and content-based filtering to make predictions
pages.summary: Recommenders build a profile of each user from their behaviour. Content-based filtering recommends items similar to ones you liked. Collaborative filtering recommends what similar users liked. Modern systems use machine learning to predict engagement, then rank items by score. They improve with more data but face problems like the cold start.
pages.starter: If you told a friend your three favourite songs, how would they choose a fourth to recommend?
sc: I can describe how machine learning scores and ranks content

b: Content-based: "You liked this, so here's something similar"
Collaborative: "People like you liked this"
Most systems combine both
Machine learning predicts a score for every possible item
Step 1: find thousands of candidates
Step 2: predict how likely you are to engage with each one
Step 3: rank by score, mix in variety, remove anything against the rules
Step 4: learn from what you do next
Cold start: new users or new posts have no data
Exploration: algorithms sometimes test new things on you
Popularity bias: popular content gets shown more and more
Feedback loops: what you're shown shapes what you click

blocks.text: Building a profile

A recommender builds a **[[user profile]]** for each person: a record of what they've watched, liked, skipped, searched for and followed, along with information such as language and location. The more you use a platform, the more detailed the profile becomes.
Two key techniques

blocks.caption: Recommendation techniques
head: Technique
Idea
Example
rows: Recommend items similar to ones you liked
You watched three cat videos, so here's another cat video
People who liked the same songs as you also liked this band

blocks.title: Collaborative filtering with three users
blocks.context: Users rated films out of 5. Aoife: Film A 5, Film B 4, Film C ? Ben: Film A 5, Film B 5, Film C 5. Cian: Film A 1, Film B 2, Film C 1.
steps: Aoife's ratings for A and B are very similar to Ben's, and very different from Cian's.
So Aoife is most similar to Ben.
Ben rated Film C 5.
blocks.answer: The system predicts Aoife will like Film C and recommends it. Real systems do this with millions of users and items at once.

blocks.text: Scoring and ranking
Modern recommenders use machine learning, trained on billions of interactions, to predict how likely you are to engage with each possible item.

items: **Candidate generation**: quickly find a few thousand items you might like from millions.
**Scoring**: predict how likely you are to watch, like or share each one.
**Ranking**: order by score, add variety, and filter out content that breaks the rules.
**Learning**: record what you actually do and update the model.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: Challenges for recommenders
items: **[[cold start|Cold start]]**: new users and new posts have no history, so the system has to guess (often showing popular content)
**[[exploration|Exploration]]**: systems sometimes show you something new to test your interest; if you engage, you'll see more
Popularity bias: popular content gets recommended more, making it even more popular
Feedback loops: you can only click what you're shown, so the algorithm partly creates the interests it measures

blocks.title: Human recommender
steps: Each person rates ten items (e.g. games, songs or snacks from the card list) from 1 to 5, leaving two blank.
Use collaborative filtering: find who in your group is most similar to you.
Predict your two blank ratings using that person's ratings.
Check how accurate the predictions were, then discuss when the method worked and when it failed.

q.q: Who was most similar to you, and how did you decide?
q.a: The person whose ratings were closest to mine on the items we both rated, e.g. the smallest total difference between our scores.

q.q: When did the method fail, and why?
q.a: E.g. when no one in the group was very similar to me, or when I have an unusual taste for one item; real systems use millions of users so they usually find closer matches.

o: Recommending items similar to ones you liked

check.q: What is the cold start problem?
o: New users or posts have no data to base recommendations on

check.q: Why do recommenders sometimes show you something new?
o: To explore and test your interests

practice.q: Explain how collaborative filtering could recommend a song.
practice.a: Finds users whose listening/ratings are similar to yours (1); looks at songs they liked that you haven't heard (1); recommends those songs to you (1).

practice.q: Explain what a feedback loop is in a recommender system.
practice.a: You can only engage with what you're shown (1), so recommendations shape the data the algorithm learns from, reinforcing what it already shows (1).

pages.title: Bubbles and rabbit holes
pages.spec: Explain filter bubbles, echo chambers and rabbit holes, and evaluate their effects on individuals and society
pages.summary: Personalised feeds can create filter bubbles, where you mostly see content that matches your existing interests and views. Echo chambers happen when communities only hear views they agree with. Rabbit holes happen when recommendations lead step by step to more extreme content. The evidence is debated, but there are real risks, especially for young people.
pages.starter: If you only ever saw posts from people who agreed with you, how would your view of the world change?
sc: I can explain filter bubbles and echo chambers
I can explain how rabbit holes can lead to more extreme content
I can evaluate the evidence and suggest ways to break out

b: Personalisation means everyone sees a different internet
A filter bubble: you mostly see content matching your interests and views
You may not realise what you're missing
Search results, news feeds and videos can all be personalised
Echo chamber: a group where everyone repeats the same views
Confirmation bias: we prefer information that agrees with us
Rabbit hole: each recommendation slightly more extreme than the last
Topics: diet and fitness, conspiracy theories, misogyny, violence
Researchers disagree about how strong bubbles are
Many people still see a mix of views
But some users, especially young people, are shown harmful content quickly
Ofcom's rules now require platforms to tame algorithms for children

blocks.text: Filter bubbles

Because feeds are personalised, two people can search for or scroll the same platform and see completely different things. A **[[filter bubble]]** is when algorithms mostly show you content that matches your existing interests and views, so you rarely see other perspectives, often without realising it.
Echo chambers

An **[[echo chamber]]** is an online space where people mostly hear opinions that match their own, repeated and amplified. **[[confirmation bias|Confirmation bias]]** (our tendency to prefer information that agrees with what we already believe) makes echo chambers comfortable. Over time, groups can become more extreme and less understanding of others, a process called **[[polarisation]]**.
Rabbit holes

A **[[rabbit hole]]** happens when recommendations lead you step by step towards more extreme content. Because algorithms are optimised for engagement, and shocking or emotional content often gets strong reactions, each recommendation can be a little more intense than the last.

blocks.caption: How a rabbit hole might develop
head: Step
What's recommended
rows: "What I eat in a day" videos from fitness influencers

blocks.text: Investigations have found that some young users were shown harmful content about self-harm, eating disorders or misogyny within minutes or hours of creating accounts, even without searching for it.

If your feed starts showing you content that makes you feel bad about yourself, scared or angry, it's not your fault, it's how the algorithm works. Use "not interested", take a break, reset your feed, and talk to a trusted adult.
What's the evidence?

Researchers disagree about how strong filter bubbles are: many people still encounter a range of views, and people also choose their own bubbles by who they follow. But there's clear evidence that harmful content can be recommended to young people. In the UK, Ofcom's children's safety codes under the Online Safety Act (in force from July 2025) require platforms to configure their algorithms to filter the most harmful content out of children's feeds.
Breaking out

blocks.title: Popping your bubble
items: Follow people and sources with different views and backgrounds
Use "not interested" or "show less" on content you don't want
Search for topics directly rather than only relying on the feed
Check where information comes from and look for other sources
Use a chronological or "following" feed when available
Reset your recommendations if your feed has gone somewhere you don't like

blocks.title: Bubble simulation
steps: Each pupil gets a different "starting interest" card and follows the recommendation flowchart for 8 rounds, picking the most "engaging" option each time.
Record the path you took and where you ended up.
Compare paths: how different were your final feeds? Did any become extreme?
Redesign one step of the flowchart to stop the rabbit hole.

q.q: Describe your path and where it ended.
q.a: E.g. started with gaming tips, then gaming rage-compilations, then videos mocking other players, then content with hateful jokes: each step more extreme because it got more reactions.

q.q: How would you redesign the algorithm to stop the rabbit hole?
q.a: E.g. add a variety rule (no more than 3 similar videos in a row), lower the score of content flagged as extreme, and give a "you've watched a lot of this, want something different?" prompt.

o: Mostly seeing content that matches your existing interests and views
A space where people mostly hear views they already agree with
Preferring information that agrees with what we already believe

check.q: What is a rabbit hole online?
o: Recommendations leading step by step to more extreme content

practice.q: Explain how a filter bubble could form.
practice.a: Algorithm recommends content similar to what you engaged with (1); over time you mostly see one type of view/interest and miss others (1).

practice.q: "Recommendation algorithms are bad for society." Discuss.
practice.a: For: bubbles, rabbit holes, polarisation, harmful content (1-2); against: help find useful content, evidence debated, people choose too (1-2); conclusion (1). Max 4.

pages.title: The attention economy
pages.spec: Explain the attention economy and identify persuasive design techniques used to keep people engaged
pages.summary: Many free apps make money from advertising, so they earn more when people spend more time on them. This is the attention economy. Designers use persuasive techniques such as infinite scroll, autoplay, notifications, streaks and variable rewards to keep users engaged. Understanding them helps you stay in control.
pages.starter: Why are most social media apps free? How do they make money?
sc: I can explain the attention economy
I can identify persuasive design techniques
I can explain variable rewards and why they're powerful

b: Most social apps are free to use
They make money from adverts
More time on the app = more adverts = more money
Your attention is what's being sold: the attention economy
Infinite scroll: no natural stopping point
Autoplay: the next video starts automatically
Notifications: pulling you back in
Streaks and badges: fear of losing progress
Pull-to-refresh is like a slot machine
Sometimes great content, sometimes nothing
Unpredictable rewards are especially hard to stop checking
Likes arrive at unpredictable times too

blocks.text: The attention economy

Most social media and video apps are free to use. They make money mainly by selling advertising, and the more time people spend on the app, the more adverts they see and the more data the company collects to target them. This is called the **[[attention economy]]**: companies compete for your time and attention, because attention is what they sell to advertisers.
Persuasive design

**[[persuasive design|Persuasive design]]** uses psychology to influence what people do. It can be helpful (reminding you to drink water) or work against your interests (keeping you scrolling when you meant to sleep).

blocks.caption: Persuasive design techniques
head: Technique
How it works
Effect
rows: New content keeps loading; there's no end of the page
Alerts, often red badges, pull you back in
Count days in a row you've used the app
Social comparison and checking for approval
Very short clips, one after another
Lots of quick rewards; time passes quickly

blocks.text: Variable rewards

A **[[variable reward]]** is a reward that comes unpredictably. Psychologists have found that unpredictable rewards are especially powerful at keeping people coming back, the same principle used in slot machines. Pull-to-refresh, notifications and likes work like this: sometimes there's something exciting, sometimes nothing, so you keep checking.
Some former tech designers have spoken publicly about regretting features they helped create, such as infinite scroll and the like button, because of how they affect people's attention.
Not all bad

Persuasive design can also help people build good habits: language-learning apps use streaks to encourage daily practice, and fitness apps use rewards to motivate exercise. The question is whether the design serves the user's goals or the company's.

blocks.title: Design detectives
steps: Look at screenshots of four (fictional) apps.
Spot and label every persuasive design technique you can find.
For each technique, decide: does it mostly help the user or the company?
Suggest a "humane" alternative for the two most problematic techniques.

q.q: Which persuasive techniques did you find, and who do they mostly help?
q.a: E.g. infinite scroll and autoplay (mostly the company: more time and adverts); streaks in a language app (mostly the user: encourages practice, but could cause stress); red notification badges (mostly the company).

q.q: Suggest humane alternatives for two techniques.
q.a: E.g. replace infinite scroll with "You're all caught up" after posts from the last two days; turn off autoplay by default with a "Watch next?" button; streaks with "freeze" days so missing one doesn't feel like failure.

o: Companies competing for people's time and attention to sell advertising
A very long scroll of paper
Content that keeps loading so there's no end

check.q: How do most free social media apps make money?

practice.q: Explain why free apps want users to spend as much time as possible on them.
practice.a: They earn money from adverts (1); more time means more ads seen/more data collected (1).

practice.q: Describe three persuasive design techniques used in apps.
practice.a: Any three, with brief explanation: infinite scroll (1); autoplay (1); notifications (1); streaks (1); likes/variable rewards (1).

pages.title: Your digital wellbeing
pages.spec: Describe how technology use can affect wellbeing and apply strategies and tools to stay in control
pages.summary: Technology can support wellbeing through connection, creativity and learning, but some patterns of use can affect sleep, mood, concentration and self-esteem. What you do online and how you feel matter more than total screen time. Tools such as screen time limits, notification settings, feed controls and quiet hours help you stay in control.
pages.starter: How do you feel after an hour of scrolling compared with an hour of gaming with friends or making something?
sc: I can describe positive and negative effects of technology on wellbeing
I can explain why what and how you use tech matters more than total time
I can use tools and habits to stay in control of my feeds

b: Positive: connection, creativity, learning, support communities, fun
Not so good: poor sleep, comparison, distraction, feeling left out
Effects differ from person to person
How you feel afterwards is a useful guide
Active use (creating, chatting with friends) vs passive scrolling
Comparing yourself with edited, filtered posts
Screens before bed delay sleep
Notifications break concentration
Screen time limits and app timers
Turn off non-essential notifications; use focus modes
Charge your phone outside your bedroom
Train your feed: "not interested", unfollow, mute, reset

blocks.text: What is digital wellbeing?

**[[digital wellbeing|Digital wellbeing]]** means using technology in a way that supports your physical and mental health. Technology isn't simply good or bad: it can help people connect, learn, create and find support, but some ways of using it can affect sleep, mood and concentration.
Quality, not just quantity
Researchers increasingly agree that what you do online and how it makes you feel matter more than total **[[screen time]]** alone.

blocks.caption: Different kinds of use
head: Type of use
Examples
Often linked to
rows: Chatting with friends, gaming together, making videos or music
Losing track of time; feeling flat
Looking at edited and filtered photos of others

blocks.text: **[[social comparison|Social comparison]]** is when we judge ourselves against others. Online, we often compare our everyday lives with other people's best, edited and filtered moments, which can make us feel worse.
Sleep

Using screens late at night can delay sleep: the content keeps your brain alert, notifications wake you, and it's easy to lose track of time. Teenagers need around 8-10 hours of sleep a night. Good **[[sleep hygiene]]** includes stopping screen use a while before bed and charging your phone outside your bedroom.
Tools and habits

blocks.title: Staying in control
items: Use built-in screen time tools (iPhone Screen Time, Android Digital Wellbeing) to see your usage and set app limits
Turn off non-essential notifications; use focus or "do not disturb" modes
Remove apps from your home screen or log out to add a pause before opening them
Train your feed: "not interested", unfollow or mute accounts that make you feel bad
Many apps now have teen accounts with time reminders, quiet hours and stricter content settings
Swap some passive scrolling for active things: making, moving, meeting friends

blocks.text: Try the "how do I feel?" check: after using an app, rate how you feel from 1 to 5. Over a week, you'll see which apps and activities leave you feeling better or worse.

blocks.title: My tech balance plan
steps: Estimate your daily screen time by activity (or check your phone's screen time tool at home).
Sort your activities into active, passive and comparison-heavy.
Do the "how do I feel?" rating for three apps or activities.
Write a personal plan with three changes, including at least one feed-control setting.

q.q: Which activities leave you feeling better or worse?
q.a: A personal answer, e.g. "Gaming with friends: better (4/5). Scrolling short videos before bed: worse (2/5), because I lose track of time and sleep later."
E.g. charge my phone in the kitchen overnight; turn off notifications from two apps; press "not interested" on videos that make me feel bad and follow more creators I learn from.

o: Using technology in a way that supports your health

check.q: What matters most for wellbeing, according to many researchers?
o: What you do and how it makes you feel, not just total time
Watching videos until you fall asleep
Charging your phone outside your bedroom

practice.q: Describe three ways teenagers can take control of their technology use.
practice.a: Any three: screen time limits/app timers (1); turning off notifications/focus mode (1); charging phone outside bedroom (1); training feed/unfollowing (1); teen account settings (1).

practice.q: Explain why passive scrolling may affect wellbeing differently from active use.
practice.a: Passive scrolling can lead to lost time/comparison/feeling flat (1); active use like chatting or creating can increase connection and creativity (1).

pages.title: Designing fairer feeds
pages.spec: Describe how laws and design can make recommendation algorithms fairer and safer, and design an ethical feed
pages.summary: Governments are starting to regulate algorithms. The UK's Online Safety Act requires platforms to protect children from harmful content in their feeds, and EU law requires big platforms to explain their recommenders and offer a non-personalised option. Fairer feeds could give users more control and transparency, and optimise for wellbeing, not just engagement.
pages.starter: If you were in charge of a video app's algorithm, what would you want it to optimise for?
sc: I can describe laws that regulate recommendation algorithms
I can explain transparency, user control and what algorithms optimise for
I can design an ethical feed and justify my choices

b: UK Online Safety Act: platforms must protect children from harmful content
Ofcom's codes: children's feeds must filter out the most harmful content
EU Digital Services Act: big platforms must explain recommenders and offer a non-profiled option
Some countries are setting minimum ages for social media

slides.t: What should a feed optimise for?
b: Engagement alone can reward outrage and extreme content
Alternatives: satisfaction, learning, connection, wellbeing
Ask users: "Was this worth your time?"
Balance relevance with variety and quality
Algorithmic transparency: explain why you're seeing something
User controls: choose topics, reset, chronological option
Independent audits of algorithms
Design with young people, not just for them

blocks.text: Regulating algorithms
Governments are increasingly making rules for recommendation algorithms:

blocks.caption: Rules about feeds
head: Law or rule
What it requires
rows: Platforms must assess and reduce risks of harm, especially to children
Platforms must configure algorithms to filter the most harmful content out of children's feeds and let children give negative feedback
Very large platforms must explain how recommenders work and offer at least one option not based on profiling
Some countries, such as Australia, have set a minimum age of 16 for social media accounts

blocks.text: Optimisation goals

Every recommender is built to maximise something: its **[[optimisation goal]]**. If a feed only optimises for engagement (time and interactions), it can end up rewarding outrage, shock and extreme content, because those get strong reactions. Alternatives include asking users whether content was worth their time, measuring long-term satisfaction, or balancing engagement with variety, quality and wellbeing.
Transparency and control

**[[algorithmic transparency|Algorithmic transparency]]** means explaining how an algorithm works and why it made a decision, for example a "Why am I seeing this?" button. **[[user control|User control]]** means giving people real choices over their feeds.

blocks.title: Features of a fairer feed
items: "Why am I seeing this?" explanations
Choose topics you want more or less of
An easy chronological or "following only" option
Reset recommendations at any time
Variety rules to avoid rabbit holes
Time reminders and a natural end point
Stronger protections and age-appropriate defaults for under-18s
Independent audits to check for harm and bias

blocks.text: Some platforms already offer some of these features, such as resetting your feed or choosing topics. A key question is whether they're easy to find and switched on by default.

blocks.title: Feed redesign challenge
steps: Your team is redesigning the "For You" feed of a (fictional) video app used by 11-16 year olds.
Choose your optimisation goal and explain why.
Design at least four features for transparency, user control and wellbeing, sketching the screens.
Check your design against the Ofcom children's codes and pitch it to the class "board", explaining how the company can still make money.

q.q: What is your optimisation goal, and why?
q.a: E.g. "Videos rated 'worth my time' by users, balanced with variety. Engagement alone rewards extreme content; asking users measures real value."

q.q: Describe two of your features and how they help.
q.a: E.g. a "Why am I seeing this?" button showing the main signals; a weekly "feed check" where users choose topics to see more or less of; after 30 minutes, a "you're all caught up, want to keep going?" screen.

check.q: What does the UK Online Safety Act require platforms to do?
o: Reduce the risk of harm, especially to children
What a recommender is built to maximise
Explaining how an algorithm works and why it made a decision

check.q: What does the EU Digital Services Act require of very large platforms?
o: Offer a recommender option not based on profiling

practice.q: Explain why optimising a feed only for engagement can cause problems.
practice.a: Extreme/shocking/outrage content gets strong reactions (1), so the algorithm promotes it, leading to rabbit holes/harm/addictive use (1).

practice.q: Evaluate whether governments should regulate recommendation algorithms.
practice.a: For: protect children, reduce harm, transparency (1-2); against/concerns: free speech, hard to enforce, innovation, user responsibility (1-2); conclusion (1). Max 4.
